blocks.text: Isaiah 2:2-4 closely parallels Micah 4:1-3: both describe Zion as the source of divine instruction, nations receiving judgment, and weapons being remade for cultivation. The relationship between the passages is debated, but the close wording makes the vision’s movement from instruction and just judgment to peace especially clear.

The opening vision includes the nations rather than limiting its horizon to Judah and Jerusalem: many peoples come to learn, and God judges between nations. This fits a wider, debated reading of Isaiah in which Judah, Israel, and foreign nations are all held accountable, while nations may also learn, worship, and share in restoration.

sections.title: The Book of Isaiah in Transmission

blocks.text: The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition while also containing thousands of spelling and substantive differences; other manuscripts from Qumran and interpretive writings show that Isaiah was actively copied and interpreted.
